```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
data_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),
                                    "../../dev/article-data/plot-sampling"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

A manager may want a stand's diameter distribution without distinguishing
species. We use the [shared simulated forest](plot-sampling-data.html), sum
tree counts over species within each diameter at breast height (DBH) class,
and fit a magnitude model together with a single ordered composition model.
We then compare predicted forest and stand DBH distributions with the known
distributions in that population.

The [magnitude article](magnitude-plot-sampling.html) estimates overall tree
density, while the [composition article](composition-plot-sampling.html)
estimates species shares conditional on known totals. Here magnitude supplies
the total and composition allocates it among DBH classes. Together they
produce a one-dimensional stand table in trees per hectare.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the plot-sampling data (ZIP)](downloads/plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="plot-sampling.zip"}

The introductory plot-sampling articles use this same archive.
Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
:::

## Sum counts within DBH classes

We read the 151 sampled plots and 4,812 prediction cells. Both tables contain
species-by-DBH counts, area in hectares, and canopy-height predictor `x`,
standardized using the plots' mean and standard deviation. We sum the plot
counts over species so the data supplied to the model have one row per plot
and DBH class, including zero counts.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

dbh_classes <- c("10-20", "20-30", "30-40", "40-50", "50+")

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(plot_id, area, x, dbh_class) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)) |>
  arrange(plot_id, dbh_class)

trees |>
  filter(plot_id == 1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Each class includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound; `50+`
contains trees at least 50 cm in diameter. Species no longer enters the
model. Summing the five counts still gives each plot's original total.

## Model total counts and DBH allocation

For plot $i$, let $N_i$ be its total count, $a_i$ its sampled area in
hectares, and $M_i$ its expected density in trees/ha. The magnitude model is

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M),
$$

where the negative-binomial distribution has mean $a_iM_i$ and size $r_M$.
The composition model allocates this total among the five DBH classes,

$$
(y_{i1},\ldots,y_{i5})\mid N_i,\mathbf p_i
\sim\operatorname{Mult}(N_i,\mathbf p_i).
$$

Here $y_{ij}$ counts trees in class $j$, and $p_{ij}$ is its probability.
As in the composition article, allocation proceeds sequentially using a
probit model. For each of the first four classes,

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi(\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}x_i),\qquad j=1,\ldots,4,
$$

is the probability of entering class $j$ among trees not yet allocated to
a smaller class. The final class receives the remainder. Each step has its
own intercept and canopy-height slope. The resulting expected density in
class $j$ is $M_ip_{ij}$, and the five densities sum to $M_i$.

## Fit and check the model

We supply DBH as the only category and give both model components a
canopy-height predictor. `magCompData()` obtains total counts by summing
the DBH-class counts within each plot.

```{r}
#| label: fit

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, category = dbh_class, tree_count = count,
  design = fixedArea(area)
)

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x,
  composition = ~ x,
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 2000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

We use default priors and automatic starting values, estimating
negative-binomial size along with the regression coefficients. Each chain
runs for 2,000 iterations and discards the first 1,000. The ordered factor
sets the allocation sequence; it does not automatically smooth coefficients
across DBH classes. Smoothing can be added through `magCompSmooth()`.

We inspect posterior estimates, 95% credible intervals, R-hat, and effective
sample size (ESS) with `summary()`. R-hat values near one indicate agreement
among chains; ESS accounts for dependence among successive draws.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-summary

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

parameter_summary |>
  select(symbol, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Parameter", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS")
  )
```

The chains agree closely for these parameters. We now assess the quantities
of interest, the DBH-class densities.

## Predict the forest DBH distribution

At each prediction cell, `target = "observation"` first draws a total count
from the magnitude model and then allocates it among DBH classes.
`type = "density"` divides those counts by cell area. We use 100 retained
draws from each chain, giving 300 joint predictions across the forest.

```{r}
#| label: predict

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, x, area),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

# Prediction cell x DBH class x retained draw x chain.
dim(predictions$density)
```

We pass these draws to `standSummary()`, which averages densities within
each draw using the cells' areas as weights. Omitting `group` produces a
forest-wide summary. The intervals include uncertainty about total counts
and their allocation among DBH classes.

```{r}
#| label: forest-summary

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)
```

To calculate truth, we sum the simulated prediction-cell counts over species
within each DBH class, just as we did for the plots. Forest density is the
class count summed across cells divided by their combined area.

```{r}
#| label: forest-truth

cell_counts <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(plot_id, area, dbh_class) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop")

forest_truth <- cell_counts |>
  group_by(dbh_class) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(area), .groups = "drop")

forest_comparison <- forest_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(dbh_class = category) |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = "dbh_class") |>
  mutate(dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))

forest_comparison |>
  select(dbh_class, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("DBH class", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%"))
```

We compare the estimated DBH distribution with the realized population
distribution. Each point estimates trees per hectare in one DBH class.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Forest DBH densities across all species. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black horizontal marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(forest_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The estimated distribution follows the population's decline in density
across increasing DBH classes. Four of the five intervals contain the true
forest densities. The `50+` class is overestimated by about 2 trees/ha,
with truth just below its interval.

## Compare stand DBH distributions

The same predictions give stand-level estimates. We read the cell–stand
overlap areas prepared in the [data article](plot-sampling-data.html#cell-areas-within-stands)
and supply `group = stand_id`. Cells crossing stand boundaries contribute
the same density draw to each stand, weighted by their area within that stand.

```{r}
#| label: stand-summary

cell_stand_areas <- read_csv("data/cell_stand_areas.csv")

stand_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = cell_stand_areas,
  unit = prediction_id,
  group = stand_id,
  represented_area = area_ha,
  summary = "samples"
)

stand_summary <- summary(stand_predictions)
```

We calculate true stand densities from the simulated cell counts using
those same overlap areas, then match them to the estimates by stand and
DBH class.

```{r}
#| label: stand-truth

stand_truth <- cell_counts |>
  mutate(density = count / area) |>
  inner_join(cell_stand_areas, by = c("plot_id" = "prediction_id"),
             relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(stand_id, dbh_class) |>
  summarise(truth = weighted.mean(density, area_ha), .groups = "drop")

stand_comparison <- stand_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(stand_id = unit, dbh_class = category) |>
  left_join(stand_truth, by = c("stand_id", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))
```

Each panel compares predicted and true density in one DBH class across all
249 stands. Points near the dashed line indicate close agreement; the
vertical bars show uncertainty in each stand estimate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stand-distributions
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true DBH-class densities across all 249 stands. Each point represents a stand, and vertical bars show 95% posterior predictive intervals. Dashed lines mark equality. Axis ranges match within each panel and vary by DBH class."

# Give both axes the same upper limit within each DBH panel.
stand_limits <- stand_comparison |>
  group_by(dbh_class) |>
  summarise(limit = max(truth, mean, q97_5), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(stand_comparison, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_blank(data = stand_limits, aes(x = limit, y = limit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ dbh_class, ncol = 3, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "True density (trees/ha)", y = "Estimated density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

The stand comparisons show differences that a forest average can conceal.
Agreement is strongest in the smallest DBH class; individual stands show
more scatter relative to their densities in the middle and larger classes.

## When species also matters

We have fitted DBH counts summed over species. If species-specific estimates
are also needed, the next article fits the
[species-by-DBH model](full-model-plot-sampling.html). Its predictions can
also produce a DBH distribution across species by summing species densities
within each posterior draw, before calculating means and intervals. This
is the DBH margin in Equation (28) of @finley2026magcompmodel.

That approach retains species information during fitting. It targets the
same DBH densities as this article, but the estimates need not be identical
because the fitted models differ.
